drills.q: Walk through a cold DNS lookup with round-trip counts, and name where clients cache separately from the recursive resolver.
drills.a: Stub->recursive resolver; if uncached, root (usually cached days via seed hints), then TLD (usually cached ~1-2 days), then authoritative -- up to 3-4 RTT cold, commonly 1 RTT in practice. Clients also cache at the OS resolver level and often the browser level, independent of whatever the recursive resolver honors.

drills.q: Why is DNS-based failover often slower in practice than its TTL suggests, and what's the fast alternative?
drills.a: TTL is advisory -- resolvers and client stacks routinely cache longer than instructed or override it. Anycast at the IP layer with BGP withdrawal on failure converges in seconds and isn't subject to arbitrary client-side DNS caching.

drills.q: Why can't you put a CNAME at your zone apex, and how do people work around it?
drills.a: The apex needs NS (and SOA) records for delegation, and DNS disallows any other record coexisting at a name with a CNAME. Workaround: ALIAS/ANAME, a provider-specific record that resolves like a CNAME but is flattened to an A record at the provider's edge, so it can coexist with NS/SOA.

drills.q: What's the actual difference between L4 and L7 load balancing, with a concrete provider example of each?
drills.a: L4 (AWS NLB) routes on IP/TCP header only, no HTTP parsing, near-zero added latency, can't route on path/host. L7 (AWS ALB) terminates TLS and parses HTTP, enabling path/host/header/cookie routing at the cost of real per-request CPU for crypto and parsing.

drills.q: Why does consistent hashing matter for a distributed cache specifically, and why use virtual nodes?
drills.a: hash(key)%n remaps nearly every key when n changes, wiping the cache; consistent hashing bounds remap to ~1/n of keys on a node join/leave. Virtual nodes (~100-200/physical node) smooth uneven arc sizes that a single ring position per node produces by chance.

drills.q: Your health check interval is 1s with a 1-failure threshold. What can go wrong, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: A brief correlated blip (GC pause, shared dependency hiccup) across many backends at once can eject a large fraction of the fleet simultaneously, dumping traffic on survivors and cascading. Fix: require N consecutive failures, stagger check timing, cap max-ejection percentage (Envoy's outlier detection supports this).

drills.q: What does sticky-session affinity cost architecturally, and what's the alternative?
drills.a: Couples requests to a specific instance, fighting horizontal scaling (can't freely add/remove instances) and complicating deploys (must drain sticky connections). IP-hash specifically hot-spots behind shared NAT. Alternative: externalize session state (Redis) so any backend serves any request -- more upfront work, pays off at scale.

drills.q: Explain anycast and correct the claim 'anycast routes to the nearest server.' Does this matter for data residency?
drills.a: Same IP announced from multiple sites via BGP; routing follows best BGP path cost (AS-path length, policy), not physical distance -- a client can be routed farther away with better peering. Yes it matters: anycast alone gives no guarantee of which region serves a client, so data residency/compliance needs explicit regional pinning on top.

drills.q: A CDN's hit rate on a personalized page matches its miss rate at scale. Diagnose the two possible causes and their relative severity.
drills.a: Either the cache key includes something per-user (session cookie, full Authorization header), fragmenting into one entry per user (a hit-rate problem), OR -- more dangerous -- the response is cached at a shared layer WITHOUT Cache-Control: private, meaning another user could be served the first user's personalized data (a security incident). Distinguish by checking whether cached entries are reused across different sessions (leak) vs never reused (hit-rate only).

drills.q: Design DNS + load balancing for a service that must fail over across regions within 10 seconds of a region going down.
drills.a: DNS TTL alone can't guarantee 10s given uncontrolled client caching. Anchor failover on anycast: announce the IP from multiple regions via BGP, withdraw on health-check failure (BGP convergence ~seconds). Use short-TTL health-checked DNS only as a secondary mechanism for clients outside the anycast network, not the primary path.

drills.q: What is origin shielding, what specific failure does it prevent, and does it add latency on the common case?
drills.a: One CDN PoP is the sole one allowed to fetch from origin on a miss; others fetch from the shield. Prevents thundering herd when a popular object's TTL expires and many edge PoPs simultaneously miss and hit origin at once. Adds small latency only on the rare miss path via the shield hop -- no added latency on the common cache-hit case.

drills.q: Why do large systems layer anycast/GeoDNS, then L4, then L7 instead of a single L7 tier for everything?
drills.a: Each layer solves a cheaper-at-its-scope problem: anycast/GeoDNS picks a region at BGP-level cost, L4 absorbs raw connection volume at near-zero per-connection cost, L7 does the expensive HTTP-aware routing only where actually needed. Collapsing to one L7 tier means paying HTTP-parsing cost for traffic that never needed content-based routing.
